title: The Afternoon Brief: Defamation, settlements, and infrastructure under strain
dek: A jury dealt the New York Times its first defamation loss in over 50 years; Israel completed reversal of its 2005 settlement evacuation while facing five-nation condemnation; courts cleared trials to proceed for an ex-CEO and ruled a former congressman mentally fit; and the Panama Canal cut capacity as El Niño tightens a critical shipping chokepoint.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: Midday brought legal reckoning for major institutions, the Times loses a rare defamation case, Mike Jeffries clears a competency hurdle before trial, and Alex Jones sees a $50 million judgment reduced on technical grounds, while geopolitical friction over West Bank settlements hardens and global shipping routes narrow.
bottom_line: Midday brought legal victories and setbacks that bypass normal institutional shields: the Times faces its first major defamation loss in decades, Jeffries clears a trial competency gate, and Jones's massive judgment faces technical reduction. Israel's settlement push hardens amid five-nation condemnation and Wahab's special election win signals mixed returns on AIPAC spending in 2026 races. A U.S. citizen faces terror charges, global shipping capacity tightens, and two criminal proceedings move toward resolution in October. Watch the Supreme Court's decision on Trump's ballroom construction, the NTSB's findings on the Alaska crash, whether Central American rainfall relieves the Panama Canal cut, and the outcome of elections in Israel on October 27.
body: The day has brought legal turns that expose vulnerabilities in institutions usually insulated from judgment. An Alabama jury awarded Kai Spears, a former University of Alabama basketball player, $9.25 million in a defamation case against the New York Times for falsely reporting he was present at a 2023 shooting. The verdict marks the first defamation loss the Times has sustained in over 50 years on a published article, according to the desk's reporting. The false claim was factual, Spears's presence at the scene, not opinion or context, and the Times did not correct it for months.

In parallel criminal proceedings, two competency battles moved past procedural gates. Federal Judge Nusrat Choudhury ruled on August 21 that Mike Jeffries, the 81-year-old former Abercrombie & Fitch CEO, is mentally fit to stand trial on sex trafficking charges, reversing an earlier incompetency finding. Choudhury based her decision on examination of medical records and over 21 hours of audio from 109 recorded calls, finding Jeffries "fluent and capable of understanding proceedings," per the desk's reporting. Trial is scheduled to begin October 26. In Kentucky, Laken Snelling, 22, a former University of Kentucky STUNT team member, pleaded guilty to first-degree manslaughter in the death of her newborn son, whose body was found in a trash bag in a closet. Sentencing is set for October 16.

A Texas appellate court cut a separate $50 million judgment against Alex Jones to $1.5 million, finding Sandy Hook parents failed to show harassment rose to a level exceeding Texas's $750,000-per-plaintiff damages cap. The ruling turns on state law structure rather than Jones's underlying liability; the $1.4 billion Connecticut judgment against him remains intact.

Meanwhile, Israel's settlement expansion and the international response have solidified. The desk reported that Israel re-established the Kadim settlement with 30 families on Thursday, completing the reversal of all four settlements evacuated in 2005. Separately, the UK, France, Germany, Italy, and Canada issued a joint statement calling Israel's decision to open construction tenders for roughly 1,234 settlement homes in the E1 area "unacceptable," with bids due October 19, days before Israel's October 27 election. State Sen. Aisha Wahab, who has called Israel's conduct in Gaza genocide, won California's special election for the 14th House District seat vacated by Eric Swalwell, defeating fellow Democrat Melissa Hernandez 53 percent to 47 percent despite a $2.5 million AIPAC-aligned super PAC campaign against her.

Global supply lines face new strain. The Panama Canal Authority announced Thursday that daily vessel traffic will fall from 36 to 32 ships starting September 15, citing low rainfall driven by El Niño. The cut affects one of the world's most critical trade chokepoints at a moment when shipping already faces disruptions from conflict in the Middle East.

On domestic security, an Albany woman, Jessica Bowie, 35, made her initial appearance on charges of attempting to provide material support to ISIS and plotting to deploy an explosive device at the New York State Capitol to kill public officials. She was apprehended on August 19 as she obtained what she believed to be an explosive device, according to the desk's reporting of the Department of Justice account. Federal agents also seized electronic devices from former Rep. Eric Swalwell as part of a criminal investigation into sexual misconduct allegations, an escalation from the congressional ethics review that ended with his resignation in April.
